articles.title: Russell Brand Says He’s “Not Guilty” in Message From Prison Read By His Wife: “Something Strange Is Happening”
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Russell Brand has shared a message from prison, delivered by his wife, Laura Brand, on his YouTube channel Sunday.

“So Russell has asked me to read something to you today,” she said at the beginning of the video, before looking to a notebook to read her husband’s message. “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”

Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault last Monday. The trial lasted four weeks at Southwark Crown Court, with the jury finding him guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault (he was found not guilty on two other rape charges and not guilty of attempted indecent assault).

Laura continued to deliver Russell’s message, reading, “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders prison in Europe.’ The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.”

“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us. Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers. Your brother in Christ, Russell,” the remarks concluded.
In a pre-recorded portion of the YouTube video, Russell compared the coverage of his trial to that of a “football match.”

“So obviously, as I said last week, we’re in the middle of a trial,” he said. “I mean, we don’t really look at coverage, but someone showed me some of the coverage the other day from people that were actually broadly supportive. But I know that’s not generally how it’s being covered in the mainstream media, and you can draw your own conclusions from that. Although what I will say is, it’s amazing to watch other people’s coverage of it because they just talk about it like it’s a football match.”
In a new report from The Times and Netflix’s Russell Brand: Open Secret documentary, six more women accused of him of alleged sexual misconduct.
Read The Hollywood Reporter‘s deep dive into the years-long road to Russell’s sentencing here.

articles.title: Governors Awards: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman Accept Honorary Oscars, Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler Receive Thalberg Award
articles.author: Scott Feinberg

paras.en: Five giants of the global film community were feted on Sunday night at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ 17th annual Governors Awards: actress Glenn Close, animator Floyd Norman and — in absentia due to a recent medical procedure — director/producer Ridley Scott with bestowed honorary Oscars, and longtime indie producing partners Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, which recognizes “creative producers whose bodies of work reflect a consistently high quality of motion picture production.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The black-tie gathering, which took place inside the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood, was, as always, packed with Academy members — including most of the 55 members of the organization’s board of governors, who host the event — and dozens of current Oscar contenders. Among them: You Can See Everything’s Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, The Odyssey’s Christopher Nolan, Zendaya, Tom Holland and Charlize Theron, The Debut’s Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti and Emma Stone, Obsession’s Curry Barker and Inde Navarrette, La Bola Negra’s Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, Elsinore’s Andrew Scott, The Invite’s Olivia Wilde and Penélope Cruz, Wild Horse Nine’s John Malkovich, Artificial’s Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, and Dune: Part Three’s Timothée Chalamet, accompanied by Kylie Jenner.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Seated with Scott were his family, along with Lucy Fisher, Doug Wick, Jim Gianopulos, Tom Rothman, Richard Lovett, Simon Halls, Steve Asbell, Matt Damon and Jerry Bruckheimer, while

Norman was notably joined by Marlon West and Travon Free. Close’s table consisted of Malkovich, Kevin Huvane, Franklin Latt, Rodrigo Garcia and Ram Bergman. Vachon and Koffler were accompanied by John Sloss, Wash Westmoreland, Marcus Hu and Liz Karlsen.

The first awardee was Norman, 91, who began his career in 1956 at Walt Disney Animation Studios as the company’s first Black animator. He contributed to numerous Disney classics including Sleeping Beauty, The Sword in the Stone, Mary Poppins, The Jungle Book and Robin Hood, as well as other notable films made outside of the Mouse House including The Hunchback of Notre Dame, Mulan, Monsters, Inc. and Toy Story 2. A friend and mentor to younger animators and storyboard artists, he was the subject of a 2016 documentary feature, Floyd Norman: An Animated Life.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Norman — only the fourth animator to ever receive that accolade, after Walter Lantz, Chuck Jones and Hayao Miyazaki — was led by Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star Mahershala Ali, who stated, “Floyd has played a pivotal role in our lives without any of us even realizing it, one [animation] cel at a time.”

In his acceptance speech, Norman reflected on his beginnings in the industry, offering “a special thank you to the best mentor a filmmaker could ever have, Walt Disney.” He concluded his speech remarking, “On occasion, even movies have a happy ending. This special evening? Here’s my happy ending.”

The evening’s next honoree was Close, one of the great stars and character actresses of the past 50 years. The 79-year-old has received eight Oscar nominations, four for leading performances (1987’s Fatal Attraction, 1988’s Dangerous Liaisons, 2011’s Albert Nobbs and 2018’s The Wife) and four for supporting turns (1982’s The World According to Garp, 1983’s The Big Chill, 1984’s The Natural and 2020’s Hillbilly Elegy). She could just as easily have been nominated for 1985’s Jagged Edge and Maxie, 1990’s Reversal of Fortune, 1994’s The Paper, 1996’s 101 Dalmatians and 1997’s Air Force One.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Close’s tally of eight noms for performances is higher than that of all but three other actresses, dead or alive — Meryl Streep (21), Katharine Hepburn (12) and Bette Davis (11), each of whom won multiple times — and more than any other living man or woman (Peter O’Toole, who died in 2013, also went 0-for-eight and received an honorary Oscar).

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Close — who previously presented honorary Oscars to the National Endowment for the Arts in 1985, Deborah Kerr in 1994 and Carol Littleton in 2023 — was kicked off by John Malkovich, who described her as “my friend and treasured colleague.” Close’s Dangerous Liaisons co-star then went on to state, “She is a true master… she’s got the goods, she can do the big stuff, the little stuff, and everything in between… Glenn is unafraid to ‘go there,’ and I love that about her,” Malkovich added. “She loves the world, she is relentless, very smart, a little cagey and a great actress who knows exactly what she’s doing and gives it 100 percent every single time.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Following a lengthy standing ovation, Close, who dedicated the award to her daughter, Annie, declared: “As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not, though some years I thought I might have a chance. I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room. Over the past 43 years, I’ve been in the room eight times… so to be in this room tonight, embraced by the people who have consistently inspired me, whose work has sustained and challenged me and only made me want to be better is the greatest honor of all.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Next up was Scott, whose films, collectively, have been nominated for 45 Oscars and won nine, but who himself has never won a competitive Oscar. The 88-year-old, who was nearly 40 when he made his directorial debut, has made up — and continues to make up — for lost time, consistently pumping out action-packed blockbusters, many now considered landmarks of cinematic achievement.

Indeed, he is behind two of the most significant sci-fi films of all time, 1979’s Alien and 1982’s Blade Runner, as well as 1991’s Thelma & Louise (for which he received a best director Oscar nom), 2000’s Gladiator (which won the best picture Oscar, while he lost best director), 2001’s Black Hawk Down (for which he received his most recent best director Oscar nom) and 2015’s The Martian. He has also produced many of his films, as well as a ton of TV series.

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Scott was led by Matt Damon, who described him as “a master at the helm” of two films they’ve made together, The Martian and The Last Duel, stating, “Thank you to the Academy on behalf of everyone who has ever worked with Ridley Scott. It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand.” Scott accepted his Oscar via a pre-recorded video from London, which included a clip from his first movie, Boy in a Bicycle, featuring his late brother, Tony, in which the narrator states, “I’ll remember this moment when I’m 80, and it’ll all seem like yesterday.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “That was a moment for both of us,” Scott stated. “Now I’m well past 80, and I’ve thought about those days and moments. It does resonate just like yesterday. Both of us sharing our first film together that led to 20 years of advertising, five decades of filmmaking… I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony. His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

The final awardees of the night were Vachon, 63, and Koffler, 60, two of the most important producers in the history of American independent film. The co-founders of New York-based Killer Films have guided to fruition all 10 of Todd Haynes’ features — including Poison (1991), Safe (1995), Far from Heaven (2002) and Carol (2015) — plus Larry Clark’s Kids (1995), Todd Solondz’s Happiness (1998), Kimberly Peirce’s Boys Don’t Cry (1999), John Cameron Mitchell’s Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001), Wash Westmoreland and Richard Glatzer’s Still Alice (2014) and Celine Song’s Past Lives (2023, for which they received their sole Oscar noms).
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Vachon, the more public-facing of the duo, has been nicknamed “the Queen of New Queer Cinema” and is such a fixture of the indie scene that she was affectionately referenced alongside Spike Lee, Michael Moore and Richard Linklater in the title of the classic 1996 tome Spike, Mike, Slackers, & Dykes: A Guided Tour Across a Decade of American Independent Cinema. Her own 2006 book A Killer Life, which she co-wrote with Austin Bunn, was included on The Hollywood Reporter‘s 2023 list of the 100 greatest film books of all time.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The presentation of the Thalberg to Vachon and Koffler was kicked off by Neil Patrick Harris with a performance from Hedwig and the Angry Inch, which Vachon and Koffler produced. Todd Haynes and Julianne Moore then conducted the actual handoff of the statuettes, with Haynes saying, “From the outside, they couldn’t see more different, and of course they are. But the ways they trade and riff off each other, divide and share their unique abilities. It’s a shimmering example of how the world might actually be if it were run by adults, otherwise known as women.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Added Moore, “These women have never been driven by profit and even recently admitted to me that no matter how hard they tried to be commercial, they’ve had to make peace of the fact that they’re just not. That doesn’t mean that they haven’t had commercial success. They are just not driven by it. They are interested in radical voices, queer voices, new voices, personal points of view.”

Vachon, in her acceptance speech, dedicated the pair’s honor to their “fellow hardworking producers,” stating, as she recalled a recent interaction, “A producer came up to me in New York and said, ‘I know this is really your Oscar, but it kind of feels like all of ours,’ And it is.”

articles.title: Dystopian Thriller ‘The Flaw’ Is a Cinematic Puzzle About Totalitarianism: “Each One of Us Is a Regime”
articles.author: Georg Szalai

paras.en: In a dark, dystopian future, the Regime decides who belongs and who doesn’t. And the Regime puts the cold and calculating Interrogator on a man who becomes the Suspect to prove his guilt. He puts a ruthless plan of psychological manipulation into action. But could there be a shortcoming in the master plan?

The dystopian thriller The Flaw, a Greece–Latvia co-production, is based on Antonis Samarakis’ novel of the same name, which is a modern Greek classic and bestseller. It is also writer-director Theophilos Papastylianos’ (Algorhythm, Showtime) feature debut, and it is about to get its world premiere, appropriately in the Baltics. The film will debut in the Baltic Film Competition of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

British talent leads The Flaw, with David Dawson, who plays Derek Jarman in Elsinore, portraying the Interrogator, and Arthur McBain (After the Flood, Napoleon) playing the Suspect. Also part of the ensemble cast are Ralf Little, Angela Brouskou, Lyne Renée, Sarah Akokhia and Georgia Small. Thodoris Zacharakis is the cinematographer, while Yannis Chalkiadakis is the editor. Produced by Panos Papahadzis and Papastylianos, the co-producers are Alise Rogule and Lina Yannopoulou. Jacques Kruger is the sales agent.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Papastylianos talked to THR ahead of the film’s premiere about just how timely and urgent The Flaw feels, its cast and visuals, and why the film is like one giant puzzle.
How did you approach adapting the novel after you read it?

It was my second time reading the book, and it was a revelation for me because the perspective was completely different. I wasn’t reading it as a teenager, like the first time. Now, I was reading it as a director.

The most important part when I wrote the script was to take a step back and say, “Okay, this is an amazing idea, but the film is going to be released in five to seven years. Is it going to be amazing in seven years?”
That said, the film feels scarily timely.

It was instinct because I was seeing how the whole world was progressing and how society was changing. I felt this book was timeless, and as the years go by, it’s going to become more up to date all the time.

The weird thing for me is that, in a sense, I’m happy that the film is up to date. But on the other hand, I’m sad because that means our society and the world are taking a very dramatic shift towards a place that is not good.
Can you talk a bit about the themes of totalitarianism and beyond that The Flaw explores?

For me, the totalitarian regimes and everything is just the first level. I wanted the film to act as a strong allegory. You have the regimes, the governments, or society, that is all around us. But I actually think that each one of us is a regime by himself.

We perceive the world through our own eyes and our own perspective, and through our own prejudice. So, by definition, we are a regime by ourselves. Imagine a hunter walking in the woods, and all of a sudden, he sees a deer. So he lifts up his rifle and looks through the scope. At that moment, he sees prey. If he could just take a moment and lower the scope, he would see a deer again. And I think it’s the same thing with people.

We meet somebody, and we judge them right off the bat – their sexual orientation, [how they look], how political or non-political they are. During COVID, for example, there were two groups of people: the anti-vaccine and the vaccine people, but nothing in the middle. But for me, that’s the interesting thing: people meet in the middle.
The two protagonists in The Flaw go through an evolution, but I didn’t fully notice it until the end…

What we were aiming for was a slow change that the characters go through. We wanted to be so slow that you realize that the characters you’ve been seeing from the beginning, all of a sudden, at the end, are completely different characters.
The film has some spectacular-looking buildings. How did you think about locations?
We shot in Greece, and we also shot in Riga in Latvia. Riga was a very important part of the whole process in order to get that feeling of brutalism and all this dark, timeless sensation.

But then we had to combine Greece with Riga, and that was a challenge, so we could get a timeless space and locations where you don’t know they were actually shot in two different countries. The production design team did an amazing job. And lighting and framing were very important for us. I believe that when we shoot, we make conscious choices that actually affect people’s subconscious.
So every shot is there for a reason. Every close-up is there for a reason. We choose what we want to show or what we don’t want to show the audience.
The Flaw features Greece and Latvia as locations. But the two lead characters are played by British guys. Tell me a bit about the casting decisions.

It was amazing to work with all these guys. They are amazing professionals. I actually sent paintings, portraits, to the casting director. And I said, “Look, this is the energy that I’m looking for as a character.” I used a lot of [Amedeo] Modigliani in terms of the paintings that I sent, because he has this energy and these figures that are surreal, but at the same time, they’re actual people.

My process with the actors once they know the scenes is this. When they ask me what I think about a scene and the characters, I always say to them, “I don’t have anything to say to you. You know the script. You know the scenes. You know your character. Just present your approach.” You need to give actors space so they can breathe on their own.
Tell me a bit about Greek theater and film actress Angela Brouskou and her role of the “Head”?

What we were aiming at was that the Head should not be a natural person but should be on the edge of becoming an idea. She represents the Regime. She is the Regime. So you have a character, but the way she’s depicted, sometimes you think that she is a non-character. It’s like she’s becoming the idea of the regime. She becomes a persona that turns into an idea.
[Warning: This question and answer contains what may be considered a spoiler.]
David and Arthur have such a fascinating dynamic and chemistry that keeps shifting. How did you approach their characters’ relationship?

For me there was a key thing. One is the alter ego of the other. So, our big challenge was to [make sure you] see hidden qualities that slowly start coming out more and more. And before the shoot, I showed them the paintings, the portraits, that [I had shared with the casting team]. And I also gave them two pieces of music they could listen to. I truly believe that our work has a lot to do with the energy of the people.
I am glad you mentioned music because that seems to play into the characters and story of The Flaw very strongly…

Yes, I got Dimitris Fessas, the composer, and we worked a lot with him. We wanted to have these rough-edged, train-like pieces. We wanted to use a lot of the electric guitar combined with violins or violas, and then he actually used a traditional Greek instrument called the Cretan lyra. There are actually scenes where the Cretan lyra is having this discussion with the electric guitar. And then a violin steps in, and the whole sensation is a little bit out of this world – in a good sense.

We created the melody of the Interrogator and the melody of the Suspect, but in the end, these two melodies have to interweave. The sound design was also an important [element of that]. We paid so much attention to every detail, especially sound-wise.
Talking to you makes me understand why I experienced The Flaw as pieces of a puzzle slowly emerging and a bigger picture coming into view.
I think that’s the best way to describe it. That’s amazing how you put it. Yeah, the whole film is pieces of a puzzle that have to come together.

articles.title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?

paras.en: China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.

That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.

While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.

"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.

The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.

"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call. The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.

Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.

China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.

"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.

Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.

U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

articles.title: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear

paras.en: Banks' third-quarter results have brought their use of artificial intelligence into sharper focus, as lenders automate routine work, reshape hiring and test whether productivity gains can translate into revenue growth.

This earnings season, Barclays unveiled layoffs in certain functions where AI is being deployed; while UniCredit and Santander said technology was freeing employees for higher-value work and improving processes. It comes as U.S. giants such as JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs make similar changes in staffing and workflows.
But as banks pursue efficiency savings, strategists say evidence that AI is generating material, demonstrable revenue gains from it remains harder to pin down.
UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel called AI an "opportunity to accelerate" that was allowing a shift toward more commercial, higher-value work and greater client engagement.
Orcel said the Italian lender — which reported its best-ever quarterly profit of 3.3 billion euros — is using the technology to "get us to the next level."
Orcel called AI "a lever that we didn't anticipate we would have, and working extremely well," on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Nov. 9.

Santander said AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026. AI is now being embedded in "all the processes that we are conducting at the bank," said Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera.

"AI basically helps, at least for now, decrease low value-added processes, and the company employees can then focus on more value-added processes — this affects both revenue and costs," Cantera told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Oct. 28.

"It's difficult to just to say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients, is helping us in asset quality, in cost management, and is having clearly a very positive impact."

Dutch lender ABN AMRO is using AI to support anti-money-laundering checks and expanding its partnership with Infosys to modernize its technology, while preserving human judgement, CEO Marguerite Bérard said in the bank's third-quarter results on Nov. 11.
"These improvements make the bank easier to run and scale, and help colleagues spend more time on activities that create value for clients," she said.

Some lenders announced big headcount reductions during the third quarter, which are "partly, but not solely, due to AI," said Andrew Stimpson, managing director and head of European banks research at KBW.
"The cuts have tended to come from back-office and support functions rather than the front office," Stimpson told CNBC via email.

Barclays said it plans to cut 5,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — in 2026. Roughly 60% of the reductions will affect support functions, including developer roles, the British lender said in its third-quarter earnings update, though it sought to emphasize that AI is not responsible for all the cuts.

The Financial Times reported on Oct. 7 that HSBC could cut around half of management and specialist roles, and as many as 70% of financial adviser roles, in its U.K. wealth business as AI reshapes how it serves clients.

Goldman Sachs said it intends to "constrain headcount growth" and cut a limited number of jobs. JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as the bank deploys AI across its businesses, CFO Jeremy Barnum told analysts in the lender's third-quarter earnings call.

A KBW study published in September examined AI use across European banks. Customer service — including chatbots and sorting customer requests — was the most frequently cited use case, followed by behind-the-scenes functions such as operations, identity checks and preventing financial crime.

Cost savings remain the most commonly cited goal: just under half of the use cases KBW tracked were aimed at cutting costs or improving efficiency. The report found banks are increasingly exploring ways to grow revenue, while noting AI is not yet seen as a major driver of profits.
Wealth management and advisory are emerging as key tests of whether AI can boost bank revenues, rather than only lower costs, analysts say.

Banks seem "fairly aligned" that they can do this in wealth management, where AI could enable advisors "to serve a larger number of clients as AI makes onboarding and reporting much more efficient," said Stimpson.

Sophia Whitbread, an analyst at Ninety One, said the evidence is still strongest for AI improving service, engagement and employee productivity, rather than demonstrably generating revenue. But initiatives that let advisors use AI to support more clients could expand access to personalized guidance without a corresponding increase in relationship managers.
She said wealth management was likely "the most important revenue test because AI can augment rather than replace the advisor."

"For European banks, the probable model is 'human adviser plus AI', especially at UBS, Standard Chartered and the private-banking units of Deutsche, ABN and the French banks, rather than a fully automated relationship," Whitbread said, pointing to JPMorgan's advisor and wealth-planning tools as a U.S. example of that approach.
AI is also reducing "traditional project management and back-office opportunities," according to Mark Astbury, a director at recruitment consultant Morgan McKinley.
There is greater demand for "specialists in AI, software engineering and data," Astbury told CNBC via email.
"London's financial services sector is increasingly becoming a technology employer. Demand for talent hasn't disappeared, but the skills banks are investing in are changing."
As AI takes on more routine tasks junior employees traditionally handle, "banks will need to rethink how they develop the next generation of talent," he said.

"We're already seeing senior roles demanding specialist AI skills that go well beyond basic use of tools like Copilot or Gemini, and I expect entry-level positions will become increasingly technical too."

articles.title: Stock futures slip as traders brace for Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO this week: Live updates

paras.en: Stock futures slipped Monday morning following a volatile week on Wall Street, as traders await a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut of Anthropic.
Nasdaq-100 futures declined 0.77%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.37%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 103 points lower, or 0.20%.

In Asia, markets were mostly lower with Japan's Nikkei 225 dropping 2.04% after third-quarter GDP unexpectedly shrank. South Korea Kospi slumped 3.48%, leading losses in the region. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.41% as well. Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.83% after downbeat key economic data, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index gained 0.94%.

Nvidia is set to report results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the chipmaker to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.

Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.

"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Another key catalyst is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each.

articles.title: The Euclid space telescope captures nearly a billion celestial objects in stunning detail

paras.en: Astronomers took a major step toward navigating the universe, thanks to the European Space Agency’s (ESA’s) Euclid space telescope, which just released its first major batch of observations.

Since its launch in July 2023, Euclid has been using its approximately 600-megapixel visible-light camera to capture images of the cosmos, near and far. All told, it has already managed to document nearly a billion objects, including more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million possible quasars, the ultrabright nuclei of galaxies where ultrahot gas is being sucked into a supermassive black hole.

Previous releases of images by Euclid had been focused on a far narrower band of sky. Now the huge amount of data collected—more than 1.7 million gigabytes—makes the new release the “largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery in a new regime for astronomy,” said ESA’s director of science Carole Mundell in a statement.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Euclid is aided in its observations by a cosmic phenomenon known as gravitational lensing. As light emitted from galaxies and other celestial objects travels through space, it interacts with the gravitational forces of other large objects. That gravity bends and magnifies the light, making it brighter and easier to detect for telescopes such as Euclid; it can even allow astronomers to determine the mass of the source. But the objects must line up just right for the lensing to occur, making them extremely rare.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: According to ESA, Euclid has identified around 15,000 strong candidates for gravitational lensing, a trove that Scott Gaudi, an astronomer at the Ohio State University, calls “bonkers.”

“Gravitational lenses are one of nature’s toolboxes for us measuring dark matter mass by looking for these distortions of background quasars and galaxies due to foreground structures,” says Gaudi, who is not involved in the Euclid program. “But you can’t do it from the ground. You just need the high-resolution imaging to do it.”

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which relies on instruments that examine infrared light, as opposed to the optical light Euclid is designed for, will also harness gravitational lensing to see far-off cosmic objects. The two approaches are “very complementary,” Gaudi says, particularly when it comes to searching for elusive things such as dark energy and dark matter.

“Euclid is going for as much area as possible, whereas Roman is focusing in the infrared, and it’s focusing on repeating observations of the same area of the sky with different roll angles and different filters,” Gaudi says. “I think the joint approach of those two missions is very powerful because you can vet the big statistics you get with Euclid with a very careful controlled system with Roman.”

Euclid’s latest release also includes a large amount of data on galaxy clusters. Examining how galaxies are bunched together can offer insights into how the first matter formed and organized shortly after the big bang. And Euclid can help astronomers begin to figure out where individual galaxies are located in relation to one another, leading to what could be the most comprehensive three-dimensional map of the universe ever made.

“Euclid doesn’t just look far back in time—it does so across huge areas of sky,” said Barbara Sartoris, an astrophysicist at France’s Joseph-Louis Lagrange Laboratory, in the ESA statement. “This gives us an unprecedented view of large samples of ancient galaxy clusters that were previously out of reach. We will explore these in the coming months to learn how these giants grew, and decipher what they reveal about the dark Universe.”

articles.title: FAA grounds all U.S. flights after air traffic control system becomes 'overwhelmed'

paras.en: On a typical Friday November evening, millions of passengers would be hopping on flights for pre-Thanksgiving weekend trips and journeys home after work. But on November 13, domestic and international flights throughout the U.S. completely ground to a halt at about 4 P.M. EST. The stop was lifted at approximately 8:15 P.M.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited a “temporary telecommunications outage,” in a post on X, and all flights have been grounded “out of an abundance of caution.” Later Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said that air traffic technology had become overwhelmed.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said at a news conference. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data,” Duffy said, adding that “they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The sweeping aviation disruption came three days after the FAA expanded its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART. The FAA previously tested the system in the National Capital Region, the airspace around Washington, D.C., in September. The artificial intelligence-driven system is intended to synthesize data on weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics in order to “reduce delays and cancellations,” according to the FAA’s description. As of November 10, it was deployed across all 22 air traffic regions in the country. At the news conference on Friday, Duffy warned that unless the country's air traffic control systems are further upgraded there may be more disruptions to air travel. Duffy called on Congress to fund upgrades to the system.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Such nationwide groundings are exceedingly rare. The last time the FAA stopped flights was for 90 minutes on January 11, 2023, to address an outage in its Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which informs pilots and operators about potential safety hazards. Before that, flights were halted immediately following the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure is managed by L3Harris, a Silicon Valley-based aerospace and defense company and a contractor for federal government agencies. L3Harris did not immediately respond to Scientific American’s requests for comment.

Ruth Stilwell, a former air traffic controller and aerospace policy expert, speculated earlier on Friday that the outage may be due to a software problem, such as a software update gone awry in the Voice Switching and Control System, which manages communications between pilots and air traffic controllers. It is not Microsoft software, Stilwell emphasizes, referring to the widespread Microsoft product outage that occurred on Thursday into Friday. CBS News reported that a software update to the private communications system may have triggered a system-wide reboot, causing it to crash.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “It would be unusual for them to do a software update during the day, but the FAA is very short-staffed,” Stilwell says. Department of Government Efficiency-related cuts laid off hundreds of FAA workers last year.

"This is yet another example of how brittle our air transportation system is in our country," says Missy Cummings, at George Mason University and a former fighter pilot whose research focuses on responsible AI in transportation. "This has been a problem over several administration, and the Trump administration made the situation much worse with all their cuts."

Even if the problem, software-related or otherwise, was small in scale, it’s standard procedure to ground planes while attempting to communicate through other channels with pilots who have already taken off, Stilwell says.

“The ground stop was the right thing to do,” Stilwell says. “Planes in the air are the top priority. The safety of those flights is way more important than anybody’s delay. The planes on the ground are safe.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Math Puzzle: Slippery slopes

paras.en: If five points are placed as shown here and straight lines are drawn between each pair of points, each line will have a unique slope. Almost all configurations of five points have this property.

Suppose you are allowed to intentionally place the five points anywhere as long as no three points can be contained in the same straight line. What is the smallest possible number of slopes that can be made by connecting pairs of points? How can you be sure?

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Challenge: What is the smallest possible number of slopes determined by any number of points? Can you prove it?

Three lines that form a triangle will always have three different slopes: if two of the lines were parallel (and thus had the same slope), they would not be able to meet up at a corner. This means the minimum number of slopes among three points that are not in a straight line is three.

Consider any configuration of five points in which no three points are in a line. Find the bottommost point and sweep out a line from it, recording the angles at which it hits the other points. If any two points share the same angle, they are both in a line with the lowest point, which means our arrangement of five points is invalid. Because that’s not allowed, we must have four unique slopes. Now draw a line from the first point you hit to the last. This line forms triangles with all the other lines and thus must give us a fifth slope—so the number of slopes is at least five. But is there a configuration with only five?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Consider the configuration where the five points form a regular pentagon:

The pairs of points form lines tracing the sides of the pentagon and all of the diagonals contained within it. Each of the sides has a unique slope. Each of the diagonals is parallel to, and thus has the same slope as, one of the sides. This gives us five slopes in total.

The answer for n points is n slopes, and in each case, the configuration that realizes this is a regular polygon. By the argument above, there must be at least n slopes among the n points. In an odd-sided polygon, each internal diagonal is parallel to a side, as demonstrated above. In the even-sided case, it becomes a bit more complicated. Sides come in parallel pairs, giving n⁄2 unique slopes from the polygon’s sides, and every internal diagonal is either parallel to a side or parallel to another diagonal that skips one point along the edge. There are n⁄2 unique slopes from the internal diagonals, which gives n slopes in total.

articles.title: Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason
articles.author: Nikk Ogasa

paras.en: This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback?
Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.
But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

articles.title: Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way
articles.author: Emily Conover

paras.en: This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback?

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

articles.title: This magic mushroom can kill
articles.author: Tina Hesman Saey

paras.en: People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.
Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

articles.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

paras.en: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

- A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.
How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.
Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections."

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon."
The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses
To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.
The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.
"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.
Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System
In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.
These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.
But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids."
More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice
After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.
Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.
These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.
The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?
Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses
To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.
Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.
The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.
Arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful."
The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.
Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?
The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come."

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.
The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.
For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.
Materials provided by Rockefeller University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Qiushuang Wu, Lara M. Seydlitz, Vladislav Iakimov, Dennis J. Hsu, Parham Habibzadeh, H. Heinrich Hoffmann, Philip B. Paty, Charles M. Rice, Sohail F. Tavazoie. Dietary arginine drives codon-dependent MHC class I translation and improves immunity in colon tumorigenesis and respiratory viral infection. Cell, 2026; 189 (19): 6012 DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.07.020

articles.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

paras.en: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
- International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research

- Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer new clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

Until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.
A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses

The newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.
Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

The latest discovery provides an important breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," said lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.
McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.
Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away
The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

According to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.
The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.
"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface."

A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.
"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away."
Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair
ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.
The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

After the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.
The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.
The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

Both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

Dr. McSweeney said, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built."
The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion."
